highlights.title: On Preprod, addresses in the README
highlights.text: Both ballots deployed with real votes, as the review asked.

highlights.title: Tell Desk
highlights.text: A new contract on Preprod running its whole lifecycle: 4 sealed reports, an acknowledged, fixed and revealed finding, and 4 privacy grades a wallet can read.

highlights.title: Fixes, verified
highlights.text: Verified patches for guessable hashes, secrets in the clear, the same tag on every action, branches and personal values, compiled and scanned again before they are offered: ballot F to B, vault F to A. Other kinds get the fix in words.

highlights.title: Share links and a README badge
highlights.text: Send a report as a link; show your grade on GitHub.

highlights.title: Real outreach, tracked
highlights.text: Public issues to 11 teams naming the file and kind of finding, and one on Midnight's examples; replies and fixes counted as they come.

highlights.title: Who pays
highlights.text: Free core. Audit-firm licenses and an ecosystem grant first, private-repository checks later; prices are hypotheses, counted from the bottom.

summary: Wave 2's review gave us a list. Every point on it is below, in the reviewer's own words, with what we did about it and where to check. Items still being built say so.

feedback.quote: To improve: Deploy to testnet and add the contract address to your README
feedback.did: Both demo ballots are deployed on Midnight Preprod with six real votes each, and the new Tell Desk contract is deployed there too. The README lists every contract address and transaction. The live page reads both ballots from the indexer and recovers 6 of 6 votes from the leaky one, 0 of 6 from the fixed one.

feedback.quote: You implemented genuine private state with implemented witnesses and a commitment/hash, exactly what a Midnight app should do.
feedback.did: We built a second contract where private state does real work. Tell Desk seals a privacy finding as a commitment with a per-report tag; maintainers answer with a zero-knowledge proof over a Merkle tree of credentials, without revealing who they are or which project; the opening is published only after the fix or the embargo. It also keeps Tell's grades by code hash for wallets to read. {tests.desk} contract tests, including an attacker who reads only public data. Version 2 is live on Preprod and has run its whole lifecycle (17 transactions): five credentials, four sealed reports, a finding acknowledged, fixed and revealed, and four grades.

evidence.label: Tell Desk: public ledger and private state

feedback.quote: We are not currently offering grants specifically, so please consider applying to our technical fellowship program
feedback.did: Applied to the Aliit technical fellowship on November 7, 2026, Builder and Educate paths, with Tell as the project. Also posted Tell as input to Midnight's MPS-0036 on review evidence (MIP discussion #413).

feedback.quote: Since the Midnight application requires an implementation that prioritizes privacy, tools like this help enhance the ecosystem's apps.
feedback.did: We took Tell to the apps themselves. The 11 teams whose contracts showed a clear finding in the survey were each sent a public GitHub issue naming the file, the line and the kind of finding, and asking where to send the details. We also filed an issue on Midnight's own examples (midnight-examples#90). Replies and fixes are tracked on the adoption page.

feedback.quote: Genuinely interesting ecosystem tool, but as a business it is small.
feedback.did: We wrote down who pays and for what. The core stays free. A hosted pull-request bot for private repositories, an audit-firm license and ecosystem sponsorship are the paid parts. Each one is marked live, pilot or planned. On November 7 we asked two audit firms to try Tell on an engagement; no reply yet, and no revenue yet.

evidence.label: Who Tell is for, and who pays

feedback.quote: Your real substitutes are the Compact compiler itself and manual review by security firms such as Trail of Bits or Least Authority
feedback.did: We answered each substitute in turn: the compiler, audit firms, the free Web2 analyzers and OpenZeppelin's Compact Security Detectors SDK. For each one we say what it does, what Tell adds and how they work together.

feedback.quote: the closest Web2 analogues (Slither, Semgrep, Snyk) are free or sold per developer seat
feedback.did: Free like them, but not sold per seat: Midnight has about 150 active developers a month, too few for seats to carry a product. The analyzer stays free and open source. Money comes from audit-firm licenses and an ecosystem grant first, and later from hosted checks priced per private repository, not per developer.

feedback.quote: the buyer pool here is the few dozen teams building on Midnight
feedback.did: For paying production teams today, that is right. The users we are building for go beyond dApp teams: audit firms, the Foundation's templates, wallets and dApp stores that read grades from the chain, and AI coding agents through the MCP server. The privacy grade becomes something users see, and that gives teams a reason to earn a good one. None of these is a customer yet.

feedback.quote: if you already have a live product, active users, or revenue, we'd love to hear from you, even if you're still early and the numbers are small.
feedback.did: Tell is live: web scanner, CLI, GitHub Action and README badge. The adoption page shows the numbers as they are, small ones included: stars, repositories using the Action, outreach replies and fixes that landed. A script reads them from GitHub's public API.

evidence.label: Adoption numbers, with the fetch date

feedback.quote: We're interested in what you've learned from bringing a product to market, what challenges you're working through, and how the Midnight ecosystem might help you take the next step.
feedback.did: Below: what we observed, how we work with teams, and the design assumptions we have not tested with users yet, each labelled as such; then what would help most from the Midnight ecosystem.

Tell reads any Compact contract, whatever the industry. We are adding worked examples from those sectors, starting with a supply-chain contract whose shipment record sits behind a guessable hash, and a game whose hidden move has only a few possible values. Each one comes with its fix.

feedback.quote: frontend intuitive, behaves as expected, connects to the contract end to end
feedback.did: The scanner now has share links (the contract travels inside the link and is never stored), a fix view with the verified patch and a re-scan, a README badge, and downloads as JSON, SARIF or Markdown. On the contract side, the read path is live in the browser: /live reads both ballots from the indexer and runs the attack, and the Tell Desk page reads reports and looks up a grade by contract address. The write path (sealing, acknowledging, revealing) runs from the Desk command-line client; a Lace wallet flow in the browser is not built yet.

substitutes.name: The Compact compiler
substitutes.what: Makes you write disclose() wherever private data may reach the ledger. It answers whether something goes public.
substitutes.answer: Tell measures how much a disclosure gives away: a hash with four possible inputs is still a disclosure. Tell reads the compiler's own reduce-to-circuit output, so it works alongside the compiler and could become one of its passes. If the compiler adopts it, that is a good outcome for Midnight.

substitutes.name: Audit firms (Trail of Bits, Least Authority)
substitutes.what: Manual review by experts, weeks of work and priced to match. Few teams on a testnet can afford it.
substitutes.answer: Tell is not competing with them. It gives an auditor a per-circuit map of every disclosure in bits, which they can use as the privacy section of a Compact review, and it gives teams that cannot afford an audit a first pass before deploying. On November 7 we asked two audit firms to try it on one engagement.

substitutes.name: Slither, Semgrep, Snyk
substitutes.what: Free or per-seat static analyzers for Solidity and general code. None reads Compact or knows Midnight's dual ledger.
substitutes.answer: We copy their model rather than compete with it. The analyzer is free and open source, like Slither. Paid hosted checks cover private code, as Semgrep's and Snyk's hosted tiers do, but priced per private repository rather than per seat, because Midnight teams are small. The difference is the domain: they find bugs, Tell measures privacy leaks in bits.

substitutes.name: OpenZeppelin's Compact Security Detectors SDK
substitutes.what: OpenZeppelin's Compact Security Detectors: two correctness detectors today, loop array bounds and verbose assertion messages. No privacy checks.
substitutes.answer: It checks correctness and Tell checks privacy, so they complement each other. Tell's output is SARIF, so both can run in the same GitHub code scanning view, and Tell's rules could feed their detectors. The benchmark runs both, with Nightshade, compact-guard and compact-lint, on the same 69 files.

learned.title: Finding the leak is not enough
learned.text: We expect a team that sees a finding to ask next how to fix it; no team has replied yet. That is why the fix view and auto-fix exist: a finding without a patch is extra work, and a verified patch is easy to say yes to.

learned.title: Privacy grades need to be seen
learned.text: A grade only on the developer's screen changes little. When a wallet or a dApp store can read it from the chain, users can see it too, and teams have a reason to earn a good one. That is the job of Tell Desk's registry.

learned.title: Tell teams before telling anyone else
learned.text: We never name a team on this site. Each team got a public GitHub issue on its own repository naming the file, the line and the kind of finding, and asking where to send the details; the details themselves are not public. This site shows only totals. A leak in a public contract is the team's to fix, not ours to announce.

learned.title: The compiler moves fast
learned.text: Several compiler releases in one buildathon, 0.36.0 and Ledger 9 among them, and the circuit form Tell reads changed shape more than once. Keeping up with each release is the main maintenance cost, and it is exactly what ecosystem support would pay for.

ask.title: A Tell check in Midnight's templates
ask.text: If create-mn-app and the example repositories shipped the Tell Action, every new project would be checked from its first commit.

ask.title: A stable compiler IR
ask.text: A documented, versioned form of the reduce-to-circuit output would make Tell, and any other analyzer, cheaper to maintain.
